upright: A transition — leaving troubled waters behind and heading for a calmer shore. It might be a move, a job change, or the end of a relationship, and sadness about what's lost travels with you. Still, the direction is toward clearer thinking and smoother water ahead. And it can be a healing journey — 'we're in this boat together' — with the support you need by your side.
reversed: The move is private and inner: quietly releasing a belief, pattern, or relationship that no longer serves you, worked on mostly alone. Or you know a change is needed and you're resisting it, hoping the problem will sort itself out. Either way, check your baggage before you set sail — carrying too much of the old story can sink the crossing. Or stuck like a car in snow, spinning its tires — no traction, no help, or help rejected.
notes: Hamaker has no Six of Swords entry, so it is omitted from sources. Papez's baggage-check warning is folded into the reversed reading. Dean: The six swords are carried, not used — self-protection on a journey, not a battle. Reed: Distinctive: Six of Swords as a healing journey, with its reversal as a return to hospital or rehab. Papez: Mix-up: Six of Swords vs Eight of Cups — escape is fleeing with help toward calm; departure is choosing to walk away uphill, alone.

name: Seven of Swords
upright: Something sneaky is afoot — deception, a hidden agenda, or someone (maybe you) bending the rules to get away with something. Trust your instincts if a situation feels off, and look honestly at your own motives too. Not every rule-breaker is a thief, though: sometimes this is rebellion against a system that deserves challenging, so check the intention before you judge. Though sometimes the oblique approach is the likelier route to success — discretion and diplomacy rather than theft.
reversed: The deception turns inward — self-deceit, or the nagging feeling that you're a fraud and don't deserve your place. It can also mean a secret you're still keeping, or a game that's ending because the truth is coming out. Honesty with yourself is the way through. Or the opposite — what feels like a big problem is an irritating delay, not a disaster.
notes: Papez reframes the card as rebellion (activists, whistleblowers) against the traditional deception reading; Clark/Gray's reversed 'unexpected good / game ends' conflicts with Esselmont's imposter-syndrome reading — both threads are kept. Adams: Reads the card as strategic cunning that can be legitimate (discretion and diplomacy) rather than only theft or deceit; reversed adds deception rather than reversing the meaning. Weber: Distinctive angle: the same card can mean burden or triumph depending on which detail your eye catches that day. Dean: The theft happens in broad daylight in a sunlit camp — daylight robbery, with stealth performed on tiptoe as parody.

name: Eight of Swords
upright: You feel trapped, boxed in by fear, indecision, or worst-case thinking — but the bindings are looser than they look. The cage is mostly built from your own thoughts, and the way out is clearer than it feels from inside. Look for the gap between the swords: help from others and a fresh angle are both within reach. Unlike the Two of Swords' denial, here you are conscious of the choices available — and still stuck.
reversed: The limiting stories start to loosen — the beliefs that told you you're too old, not deserving, or unable to change begin to lose their grip. Catch the thought pattern, question it, and try an unexpected way out. Freedom here starts in the mind, and it is genuinely possible. Though Adams warns the reverse can also mean what is already wrong getting worse — get your affairs in order.
notes: Sources agree unusually well here: Esselmont, Papez, Clark, and Gray all point to a self-imposed trap with a real escape. Adams: Distinctive contrast with the Two of Swords (denial vs. conscious paralysis), and the hopeful note that a future-position Eight of Swords can still be avoided. Weber: Distinctive angle: the 8 of Swords as a self-made cage with loose bindings — the escape is already available. Dean: Distinctive angle: Dean names the woman in orange as the Other, the witch — the card's restriction is also about who is allowed to be free. Papez: Mix-up: Eight of Swords vs Devil — overwhelm is self-imposed by thought; bondage is attachment to something outside you.

name: Nine of Swords
upright: Anxiety and worry piling up, especially in the small hours — fears stack on each other until they feel like facts. The thoughts are loud, but they aren't necessarily true, and acting from them can turn a fear into a self-fulfilling prophecy. Name what's actually frightening you, and check which fears hold up in daylight. Weber calls it the 'crying in the bathtub' card — it may mirror your catastrophizing more than any fact.
reversed: The spiral deepens and things feel much worse than they really are, with fear draining your energy and stealing your rest. Get a reality check from someone you trust, confide in them, and start letting go of the beliefs that keep the cycle turning. Tomorrow really is another day. Or the opposite reading: the nightmare ends at last, the pain is over, and with support you can move on.
notes: Gray's reversed reading (patience, time brings healing) conflicts with Esselmont and Clark, who read reversal as heavier turmoil — majority reading chosen, with Gray's healing thread kept in the closing line. Weber: Distinctive angle: the 9 of Swords as a mirror of a querent's own catastrophizing — it may reflect fear more than fact. Dean: The bedspread is daytime perspective — the card contrasts the night's anguish with how it will look in daylight. Reed: Distinctive: Nine of Swords reversed as leaving hospital/rehab or receiving effective therapy.

name: Ten of Swords
upright: A painful, final ending — a relationship cut off, a job lost, a plan in ruins. It hurts, and there's no softening that, but this is rock bottom, which means the pain has nowhere further to fall. The sun is already rising in the image: this is the end of the pain, not the end of you, and a new beginning is on the horizon. And the swords can read as acupuncture needles — painful, but placed to heal; defeat teaches a better way to win.
reversed: You're resisting an ending that has already happened, and holding on only drags the pain out longer. Letting go — ripping off the bandage, painful as it is — is what lets recovery begin. What looks like ruin also clears the ground for something new. Or pick yourself up and start fresh — the swords have fallen out, and nothing holds you back from a new life.
notes: Gray's reversed reading (overthrow of evil, courage to rise again) conflicts with Esselmont and Clark (resisting the ending / bitter ending) — synthesis keeps the resistance theme and folds Gray's rising-again into the close. Weber: Distinctive reframe: the 10 of Swords as acupuncture and a sunrise — strategy, strength, and appreciation hidden in defeat. Dean: The light over the mountains may be sunset or sunrise — night and day together mean coming light, not just ending. Reed: Distinctive: Ten of Swords as back trouble or surgery, with its reversal as rebirth after the ending.

name: Page of Swords
upright: Curious, questioning, full of fresh ideas — a perpetual student who wants to know how things really work and won't settle for 'because I said so.' You're in the exploring phase: gathering information, asking sharp questions, and spotting what others miss. The energy is real, even if mastery is still ahead of you.
reversed: You're holding back from speaking your truth out loud, keeping it private — or you're all talk and no follow-through, promising more than you can deliver. Ethony's shadow is the immature detective: disappearing into your own head, unable to trust or be trusted. Speak up, but only promise what you can actually do. Though reversed can also mean privacy — keeping motives quiet — rather than deception.
notes: Ethony's archetype: The Detective — curious, perceptive investigator. Hamaker warns the Page's rashness can cut down new options before they grow. Weber: Distinctive angle: the reversed Page of Swords can mean privacy or keeping motives quiet, not only deception. Dean: Ten birds in the sky are messages and worries — the Page's mental weather made visible. Papez: Court sliding scale: strengths are curiosity and clear thinking; struggles are nosiness and tactlessness.

name: Knight of Swords
upright: Driven, fast, and fiercely focused — once your mind is set, nothing slows you down. You charge ahead with intellect and determination, solving problems and defending what you believe in. It's powerful energy; just make sure the cause is worth the charge.
reversed: All that energy with nowhere good to go — restless, frustrated, making rash and impulsive decisions, changing your mind and confusing everyone around you. In shadow this becomes the aggressive warrior: acting without thinking, punishing without cause. Slow down enough to aim before you charge. But a reversed Knight is never a dead end — the charge can be redirected rather than abandoned.
notes: Ethony's archetype: The Warrior — swift, fearless defender. Papez's sliding scale runs ambitious to ruthless; Hamaker notes the quarrel can sometimes bring relief. Weber: Distinctive angle: reversed Knights are never a dead end — the charge can be redirected rather than abandoned. Dean: Birds and butterflies in his wake are thought itself — the Knight's charge is mental before it is physical. Papez: Court sliding scale: strengths are drive and mental clarity; struggles are ruthlessness and impatience with anything slow.

name: Queen of Swords
upright: Clear-eyed, independent, and fair — you lead with your head, see straight through nonsense, and judge situations without sentimentality getting in the way. Your sharpness comes from experience, and your advice is worth listening to. You connect through honest understanding, not flattery. And she can be a surgeon or mental health practitioner — a professional who speaks up for you.
reversed: Your emotions are clouding your usually clear vision, or relationships are pulling your decisions off course. The sharp mind can also turn inward as self-criticism and unreasonable demands, or outward as cold, cutting judgment. Step back, look at things objectively, and be firm without being cruel. And in older books this is the widow's card — loss and grief suffered in silence.
notes: Ethony's archetype: The Judge — fair, razor-sharp truth-teller. Papez's sliding scale runs perceptive to judgmental; Place's stern, cloud-caped queen echoes the same cool authority. Weber: Distinctive angle: Weber's code reads the Queen of Swords as respect (especially for women), leadership, and challenging the status quo. Dean: The two sickles on her throne are divine judgement, and the red bracelet is Venus — mercy and redemption worn by the sternest queen. Reed: Distinctive: Queen of Swords reversed as the widow's card — loss and grief suffered in silence. Papez: Court sliding scale: strengths are perception and honesty; struggles are harsh judgment and coldness.

name: King of Swords
upright: Intellectual authority and clear judgment — you think things through like a chess player, weigh all the factors, and then decide firmly and fairly. You express yourself with clarity, stand by your convictions, and keep emotions from muddying the call. It's the mind at its most mature and useful. Weber's code reads him as independence and self-sufficiency — a great ally but a terrible enemy.
reversed: Power misused, or logic taken too far — coldness, arrogance, and manipulation when the sharp mind runs ahead of care for people. Esselmont also notes a quieter side: authority that comes from within, not from volume. The invitation is to lead with principle, not ego, and to leave room for feelings and intuition.
notes: Ethony's archetype: The Scientist — brilliant, visionary logician. Esselmont's 'quiet power' reversed reading is unusual and is kept alongside the traditional misuse-of-power thread. Weber: Distinctive angle: Weber's own code reads the King of Swords as independence and self-sufficiency — a great ally but a terrible enemy. Dean: Two moons on his throne are cycles and phases — even the King of logic answers to timing. Papez: Court sliding scale: strengths are strategy and rational judgment; struggles are emotional detachment and rigidity.

name: Ace of Pentacles
notes: Hamaker adds giving a gift concrete form, often the start of a relationship; Clark and Gray warn that greed and mismanagement spoil the opening. Weber: Distinctive angle: Weber's student read the reversed Ace of Pentacles as an expensive secret tied to home. Dean: The rose arch is a transition — the Ace's garden is a threshold, not just a prize.
reversed: The opportunity may be slipping, stalling, or not quite what it seemed — hesitation, distraction, or a door closing before anything lands. It can also point to greed or sloppy handling spoiling a good start. Wait until things are solid before counting on them, and check honestly whether fear or carelessness is getting in the way. Or a loss kept quiet, particularly around house and home — an expensive secret.
upright: A real, tangible opening is here — a job, a bit of money, a chance to build something solid — and the groundwork you have already laid helped bring it about. It is a green light, not a gift: the seed is in your hand, and what grows from it depends on the steady effort you put in next. Take the chance seriously, and give it your full attention rather than scattering it. Weber's keyword for the Aces is 'absolute': absolute opportunity — the suit of the body and material life at full strength.

name: Two of Pentacles
notes: All sources agree: upright is balance held at capacity, reversed is the balance breaking. Papez frames it as priorities — the only anchor is deciding what comes first. Dean: The green rope forms the infinity symbol — the juggle itself is flow and energy, not just strain. Papez: Mix-up: Two of Pentacles vs Temperance — juggling separate priorities versus mixing two extremes into moderation.
reversed: You are overcommitted and starting to drop things, with an overloaded schedule or bills that will not stay on top of themselves. It may also mean pouring everything into one area while the rest quietly falls apart. Get organised, reprioritise, and turn down what no longer fits — the juggling only works when something is allowed to wait.
upright: You are juggling several priorities at once — work, home, care for yourself — and managing the balance well, dancing on one foot while the sea stays rough behind you. The line between coping and losing control is thin, though, and you are close to capacity. Decide what comes first in any given moment, and remember that rest is productive too.

name: Three of Pentacles
notes: Clark's number theme: progress — hard work earns its just reward and growth endures. Place reads it as creative work for a salary or commission inside an established organisation. Dean: Distinctive angle: the uncarved stone is future potential, and the crypt itself is foundations — the building is the message.
reversed: Disharmony is stalling the work — people not listening to each other, ego getting in the way, or someone biting off more than they can chew. It can also mean the skill itself is not there yet, or effort being abandoned before it pays off. Come back to the original shared goal, renegotiate how you work together, and plan more carefully before pushing on.
upright: Working together creates something no one person could build alone: the stonemason, the planners, the patron each bring a different skill, and mutual respect turns those differences into something lasting. This is skilled work taking real shape — learning on the job, earning your reward, and growing through the collaboration itself. Keep going with confidence; the plan is coming together.

name: Four of Pentacles
notes: Sources conflict on the reversal: Esselmont reads it both ways (release or overspending) and Gray leans toward the spendthrift and setbacks; both readings are carried here. Hamaker: trustworthy and stable, but nothing vital or inspired while the grip holds. Dean: The hand position — a coin held at the heart — is read as money at heart, the card's core image.
reversed: This one reads two ways, and both are worth sitting with. It may mean loosening your grip — realising money and possessions will not make you happy, and letting go of what you have been guarding. Or the opposite: money slipping through your fingers as spending outruns saving. Either way, the question is the same: what is the holding-on actually protecting?
upright: Look honestly at your relationship with money. At its best this is wise saving — protecting what you have built with caution and discipline. More often it is a scarcity mindset: clutching every coin because you fear there will never be enough, and building walls that keep other people and new growth out. Seeds kept safe and dry never grow more fruit.

name: Five of Pentacles
notes: All sources agree on the lit-window image — aid offered but unseen. Esselmont alone adds the reversed nuance of an inner, spiritual poverty persisting past material recovery. Dean: Distinctive angle: Dean reads this as poverty consciousness — fear of poverty — as often as actual lack, and the window as sanctuary unnoticed. Reed: Distinctive: Five of Pentacles as hope just around the corner despite hardship, and its reversal as a return to hospital or rehab.
reversed: The difficult stretch is easing — new income, a new job, or help arriving — and hope and self-confidence are coming back with it. Support is found, and persistence carries you through. Even so, check for a quieter poverty underneath: something can still feel missing, even once the material pressure lifts.
upright: Hard times have stripped something away — a job, a home, a sense of security — and you feel left out in the cold, walking past a lit window without noticing it. The help is closer than it feels, but pride or a lack mindset can make a temporary hardship feel permanent. This is a Minor Arcana card, not a life sentence: this too shall pass, and admitting you need a hand is part of getting through it.

name: Six of Pentacles
notes: Sources agree on reciprocity upright; they split on the reversal — Esselmont stresses one-sided giving and self-care, Gray stresses purse-pride, bad debts, and gifts given as bribes. Hamaker: the old cycle of becoming a success is over, and wealth must now be used ethically. Dean: The scales in the giver's hand are mercy and precision — giving as a measured, just act, not a casual one. Reed: Distinctive: Six of Pentacles reversed as a contested will or unfair inheritance, and as the caregiver becoming the one who needs care.
reversed: Check the balance of the flow. You may be giving and giving while others take without returning, leaving you feeling used — or giving to everyone except yourself after a long stretch of generosity. Make sure you are included in your own care — and watch the money itself, too: an unfair inheritance, a contested will, or a caregiver who now needs care themselves. At its worst this is giving with strings attached, or prosperity propped up by bad debts.
upright: Giving and receiving flow both ways here — the merchant weighing coins fairly, sharing with those who have less, knowing the cycle turns and everyone gives and takes in turn. You may be the one with more than enough right now, ready to pay it forward with money, time, energy, or wisdom. Or you may be the one who needs to let pride drop and accept the help being offered.

name: Seven of Pentacles
notes: Conflict: Gray reads the upright far more pessimistically (unprofitable speculation, loss, disappointment, success not attained) while Esselmont, Papez, and Hamaker all read it as patient evaluation — the majority reading is used here. Dean: Seven of fourteen in the suit: Dean reads it as the halfway point, when doubt sets in — the card's position in the suit is part of its meaning.
reversed: Your efforts feel scattered, and you are questioning whether you invested in the right things — spending on what bears no fruit, or pouring energy in without the rewards you expected. Impatience creeps in, and so does the worry over things you can no longer change. Pause, prioritise, and do an honest cost-benefit check before planting anything more.
upright: This is the gardener's pause: step back from the daily work, look at what has actually grown, and ask whether your time and energy are going to the right places. The seeds are planted and the cake is in the oven — too late to change course, too early to know the harvest — so trust what you have done and let time do its part. You are playing a long game here, not chasing a quick win.

name: Eight of Pentacles
notes: Esselmont and Papez both name the perfectionism and impostor-syndrome shadow; Gray goes further, warning of skill turned to cunning. Place and Hamaker stress the apprentice's steady, motivated work. Dean: The finished coins are displayed on a tree — growth and measurable progress shown together.
reversed: Perfectionism may be getting in the way — nothing ever feels good enough, and the bigger picture disappears behind the details. Or the work has gone stale: boredom, monotony, or stagnation despite all the effort, and a feeling of being your own worst critic. Mastery can lock you into a path you no longer want, so check whether the craft still serves you.
upright: This is apprenticeship and mastery: the craftsman at the bench, repeating the work until skill becomes second nature. Diligent, focused effort is producing real excellence, and further study or practice will only deepen it. The work itself is the teacher — keep showing up, keep refining, and the results will follow.

name: Nine of Pentacles
notes: Sources split on the reversal: Esselmont frames it as self-worth and overwork, Gray as a cancelled project or loss of home or friendship — both are carried here. Hamaker: rest and movement together, wholeness without stagnation. Weber: Distinctive angle: the 9 of Pentacles' serene surface with a forlorn undertone — abundance with something unsaid. Dean: Distinctive angle: the snail at her feet — slowness and protection — is Dean's emblem for enjoying wealth without rushing.
reversed: This turns into a self-worth question. You may doubt you are enough, under-charge for what you do, or accept less than you deserve. Or the balance tips the other way — hustling so hard for more that you never stop to enjoy what you already have. Slow down, and check whether a project or friendship is quietly being lost while you chase the next thing.
upright: You have worked hard and the harvest is yours to enjoy — comfort, leisure, and the quiet pleasure of a garden you tended yourself. This is abundance earned through independent effort, discipline, and self-confidence, and it comes with room to breathe: enough to feel safe, and enough to stretch your wings. Treat yourself; you have earned the rest. Yet something forlorn may sit underneath the serenity — comfort is real, but so is the quiet conflict, a confidence not yet spoken.

name: Ten of Pentacles
notes: Sources split on the reversal: Esselmont asks whether the conventional wealth-and-family dream is truly yours, Gray warns of family misfortune and loss of inheritance — both are carried here. Clark's number theme: completion. Weber: Distinctive warning: the 10 of Pentacles reversed as a caution against showing your full hand. Dean: The ten coins are read as the world itself — the whole suit's journey arriving at legacy.
reversed: Ask whether this picture of stability, security, and commitment is truly what you want — or what is expected of you. Wealth can become a trap, always wanting more and never feeling satisfied, and the foundations may not be as solid as they look. Family strain, a lost inheritance, or a poor-risk venture can also unsettle the legacy, so move carefully with money that involves others. And keep your money close — do not reveal all of your strengths right away.
upright: This is the full picture: wealth, a stable home, family across generations, and the long-term security that comes from plans carried through. It is the apex of the suit — not just money, but a legacy, the lasting mark you leave and the resources, knowledge, and care that outlive you. Matter and spirit walk hand in hand here: enjoy what is real and unadorned, and share the abundance with others. Though wealth brings its own questions — taxes, responsibilities, whether it will stay.

name: Page of Pentacles
notes: Ethony's archetype: The Naturalist — a quiet, gentle soul happiest among animals and nature. Papez: diligent to perfectionistic, the Magician of earth. Clark: introvert Pentacles youth — responsible, reliable, logical. Weber: Distinctive angle: any reversed Page means there is more to the story — withheld truth or something hidden. Dean: The coin is held delicately, almost reverentially — talent and reward treated as precious, not spent. Papez: Court sliding scale: strengths are diligence and a love of learning; struggles are perfectionism and fear of not measuring up.
reversed: The idea is stalled — kept secret, endlessly brainstormed, or put off for fear you lack the skills — or your efforts keep amounting to nothing and need a fresh plan. Perfectionism can freeze the momentum here, sweating the details while the bigger picture waits. In shadow this gentle learner withdraws, struggling with boundaries and with saying what they need. And any reversed Page means there is more to the story — withheld truth or something hidden.
upright: A new material opportunity is opening — a job, a course of study, a project to build — and you are approaching it like a careful student, eager to learn and ready to work. This is earth of earth, the most grounded of the court: practical, diligent, happiest learning through touch and patience, wanting real, measurable results from the effort. Dive in and receive what comes, without worrying yet about the end result.

name: Knight of Pentacles
notes: Ethony's archetype: The Soldier — the loyal, duty-bound protector who keeps going long after everyone else has left. Papez: dependable to inflexible, the Chariot of earth; Hamaker: caution and perseverance, but conservative and passive, with little vision for the future. Weber: Distinctive angle: the Knight of Pentacles as a 'battle of enterprise, not conflict' — determination in work and money. Dean: The coin is read as a seed the Knight is about to plant — the slowest knight is the one thinking furthest ahead. Papez: Court sliding scale: strengths are reliability and persistence; struggles are stubbornness and resistance to change.
reversed: The steady pace has hardened into stuckness — boredom, complacency, or a routine that no longer leads anywhere, and a self-development journey that needs real structure. In shadow this loyal worker turns rigid and perfectionist, following authority without question and losing themselves in duty. Check whether discipline is serving the goal, or has quietly become the goal.
upright: Slow, steady, and reliable: you have a plan, you stick to your routine, and you finish the job one foot in front of the other. This is the only knight whose horse stands still — not fast or flashy, but loyal, patient, and committed to the long haul, protecting the people you love by simply keeping going. Trust the methodical pace; it gets there.

name: Queen of Pentacles
notes: Ethony's archetype: The Healer — the warm, nurturing comforter. Papez: comforting to enabling, the Empress of earth. All sources agree on the nurturing provider; the reversal is where the shadow (control, enabling, self-neglect) lives. Weber: Distinctive angle: the Queen's love shown through practical giving, and the risk of practicality crowding out feeling. Dean: The rabbit on her throne is nature's cycles, and the ground beneath her is uncultivated — she is still doing the groundwork. Papez: Court sliding scale: strengths are practical care and warmth; struggles are over-protecting and enabling dependency.
reversed: Turn that caring energy toward yourself for once: build the financial independence that lets you sustain your own life, and nurture yourself with rest, good food, and retreat, knowing others can manage while you care for you. In shadow the caring curdles — smothering control, enabling what harms, or manipulating others while denying your own need to be cared for. Mistrust and neglected duties can follow when the giving runs on empty.
upright: Warm, practical, and generous — the caretaker of the material world, who looks after home and family while also earning and creating abundance. She holds her community together, stays steady in a crisis, and gives through tangible, useful support: good food, sound advice, a safe place to land. She is a caretaker of her wealth rather than its owner, enjoying the good things of the earth with restraint. Though she may place money or practicality over emotion.

name: King of Pentacles
notes: Ethony's archetype: The Manager — the dependable, wealth-building provider. Papez: wise to cynical, the Emperor of earth. Clark: introvert Pentacles adult — moderate, careful, content. Weber: Distinctive angle: reversed Kings/Queens as unfulfilled potential; reversals can also signal secrets. Dean: The boar on his throne is base instincts kept in check — the King's wealth includes his appetites. Reed: Distinctive: King of Pentacles reversed as money used as a weapon, and as the 'Bernie Madoff type' who profits while harming others. Papez: Court sliding scale: strengths are wisdom and sound management; struggles are cynicism and measuring everything by its price.
reversed: Look honestly at the relationship with money. It may be mismanagement — earning well but spending just as fast, gambling on high-risk ventures, or letting thrift slide into waste. Or it may be worship: money put before relationships, wellbeing, even integrity, with a cynical edge that trusts slowly and resists change. In shadow the provider turns greedy, critical, and impatient, feeling there is never enough — or money becomes a weapon, used to harm while profiting, the miser who hoards what others need.
upright: A wise, steady provider who built wealth through experience and knows how to keep it growing: practical, reliable, slow to anger, and generous with those under his care. He spots risks before others do, plans for the fallback, and turns vision into something tangible and lasting. This is success that enjoys the earth's gifts without taking them at anyone else's expense.
